hints: Think about what type of structure each of $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{Si}$ and $\text{P}$ has, metallic giant, covalent giant or simple molecular.
Recall how melting point changes across the three metals as charge on the ion and number of delocalised electrons increase, then what happens at silicon.
Remember why there is a very large drop from silicon to phosphorus, think about what forces you are overcoming in each case.
walkthrough:
Picture the bonding in the first three elements**
$\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Al}$ are all metals with giant metallic lattices. Melting means loosening the attraction between positive ions and the sea of delocalised electrons. From $\text{Na}^{+}$ to $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Al}^{3+}$ the ionic charge increases and more electrons are released per atom, so the attraction gets stronger. That is why your line must rise from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Mg}$, with only a small further rise to $\text{Al}$.

Place silicon at the top**
$\text{Si}$ has a giant covalent structure with strong $\text{Si-Si}$ covalent bonds in three dimensions throughout the crystal. Breaking that network takes far more energy than loosening metallic bonding, so $\text{Si}$ has the highest melting point of the five. Draw a sharp rise from $\text{Al}$ up to $\text{Si}$.

Drop sharply to phosphorus**
$\text{P}$ exists as discrete $\text{P}_{4}$ molecules held together only by weak London dispersion forces. You are no longer breaking strong metallic or covalent bonds, only weak forces between molecules. So melting point falls dramatically from $\text{Si}$ to $\text{P}$. Label every point clearly on the $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{Si}$, $\text{P}$ axis.

Final answer: Sketch showing: $\text{Na}$ lowest, rising to $\text{Mg}$; $\text{Mg}$ to $\text{Al}$ slight rise then sharp rise to maximum at $\text{Si}$; sharp fall from $\text{Si}$ to $\text{P}$. All five points labelled $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$, $\text{Si}$ and $\text{P}$.

hints: Compare the bonding in $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{PCl}_{5}$, one is a giant ionic lattice, the other is a simple covalent molecule.
Think about the difference between simply separating hydrated ions in water and actually reacting with water to break $\text{P-Cl}$ bonds.
Recall what solution you get when $\text{HCl}$ gas dissolves in water, and which chloride will produce $\text{HCl}$ on contact with water.
walkthrough:
Sort out the starting states**
Both chlorides are solids at room temperature. $\text{NaCl}$ is a giant ionic lattice solid, high melting point. $\text{PCl}_{5}$ is a covalent solid that exists as ions in the solid but sublimes easily, still solid under room conditions. So write solid for both.

Separate dissolving from reacting**
When $\text{NaCl}$ meets water, water molecules pull the $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions apart and hydrate them. No bonds inside water are broken and no new acid is made. We call this simply dissolving:
$$\text{NaCl(s) + aq} \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}\text{(aq) + Cl}^{-}\text{(aq)}$$
When $\text{PCl}_{5}$ meets water it reacts vigorously. $\text{P-Cl}$ bonds break and $\text{O-H}$ bonds in water break to form new $\text{P-O}$ and $\text{H-Cl}$ bonds. We call this hydrolysis, for example:
$$\text{PCl}_{5}\text{(s) + 4H}_{2}\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}\text{(aq) + 5HCl(aq)}$$.

Predict the pH from the products**
Hydrated $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ do not react with water to make $\text{H}^{+}$ or $\text{OH}^{-}$, so the solution stays neutral, pH 7.
Hydrolysis of $\text{PCl}_{5}$ produces strong acid $\text{HCl}$ plus phosphoric acid $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$, both release $\text{H}^{+}$, so the solution is strongly acidic, pH 1 to 2.

Final answer: sodium chloride: solid at room temperature, dissolves on addition of water, pH 7 of final solution.
phosphorus(V) chloride: solid at room temperature, hydrolysis on addition of water, pH 1-2 of final solution.

hints: Recall what happens when $\text{Br}_{2}$ is added to $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{NaBr}$ and $\text{NaI}$ in the normal halogen displacement experiments.
Think about how oxidising power of $\text{X}_{2}$ and reducing power of $\text{X}^{-}$ change down Group 17, and where $\text{Ts}$ sits relative to $\text{Br}$.
walkthrough:
Use the familiar halogen pattern**
You know that a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide: $\text{Cl}_{2}$ displaces $\text{Br}^{-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$, $\text{Br}_{2}$ displaces $\text{I}^{-}$ but not $\text{Cl}^{-}$. Reactivity as an oxidiser decreases down the group. $\text{Ts}$ is below astatine, so far below bromine. That makes $\text{Ts}_{2}$ a much weaker oxidiser than $\text{Br}_{2}$, and $\text{Ts}^{-}$ a much stronger reducer than $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Write the displacement and explain it**
So $\text{Br}_{2}$ will oxidise $\text{Ts}^{-}$ to $\text{Ts}_{2}$ while it is itself reduced to $\text{Br}^{-}$:
$$2\text{Ts}^{-} + \text{Br}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{Br}^{-} + \text{Ts}_{2}$$
With sodium spectator ions:
$$2\text{NaTs} + \text{Br}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{NaBr} + \text{Ts}_{2}$$
The explanation is that reducing strength of the halide ion increases down Group 17, so $\text{Ts}^{-}$ readily gives electrons to $\text{Br}_{2}$.

Final answer: equation: $2\text{NaTs} + \text{Br}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{NaBr} + \text{Ts}_{2}$
explanation: $\text{Ts}^{-}$ reduces $\text{Br}_{2}$ / $\text{Br}_{2}$ is displaced because reducing strength of halide ion increases down Group 17.

hints: Look at the given values, $-101$ for chlorine and $-7.2$ for bromine, and think about the normal trend in London dispersion forces down Group 17.
Consider what completely different bonding and packing copper has compared with solid $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and $\text{Br}_{2}$, and what that means for melting point and lattice name.
walkthrough:
Keep chlorine and bromine as simple molecules**
Solid chlorine and solid bromine both consist of discrete $\text{Cl}_{2}$ and $\text{Br}_{2}$ molecules held by weak London dispersion forces. We describe this packing as simple molecular. Their melting points are low and already given as $-101^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $-7.2^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Give tennessine a metallic character**
If $\text{Ts}$ behaves like copper, it no longer forms discrete $\text{X}_{2}$ molecules. It forms a giant metallic lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons with strong non directional bonding. Metallic bonding needs a lot of heat to break, so predict a high melting point typical of a metal, well above $250^{\circ}\text{C}$, and label the lattice as giant metallic.

Final answer: melting point: chlorine $-101^{\circ}\text{C}$, bromine $-7.2^{\circ}\text{C}$, tennessine $>250^{\circ}\text{C}$.
lattice structure: chlorine simple molecular, bromine simple molecular, tennessine giant metallic.
